title: Order to Take Every Course
statement:
A school offers n courses, numbered 0 to n - 1. Each entry rules[i] = [a, b] means course a must be finished before course b can start. Rules may repeat.

Return an order in which you can take all n courses, one at a time, so that every rule is respected. The order must list each course exactly once, including courses that appear in no rule. If no such order exists, return an empty list [].

Usually many orders are valid. Any valid order is accepted.

examples.why: 2 must come first and 3 last. 0 and 1 do not depend on each other, so [2, 1, 0, 3] is just as correct.
The three courses wait on each other in a circle, so no order works. A partial order such as [0, 1] is wrong: the answer is all or nothing.
Course 2 has no rules but must still appear. [2, 1, 0] and [1, 2, 0] are also correct.

hints: Which courses can you take first, before anything else?
Once you take a course, its rules no longer block anything. Which new courses become free?
Keep a count of open rules per course. Repeatedly take any course whose count is 0 and lower the counts of the courses it unlocks. If you cannot reach n courses, there is a loop: return [].

explain.intuition:
An order that respects every arrow a → b is called a topological order. It is what a build tool computes before compiling modules, or what a spreadsheet computes before recalculating cells that depend on other cells. It exists exactly when the arrows have no loop.

Kahn's algorithm builds the order directly: the courses with no incoming arrows can go first; write them down, delete their arrows, and repeat with whatever became free. The order in which courses leave the queue is a valid answer. If the queue empties before all n are written, the leftovers sit on or behind a loop, and the answer is []. A DFS also works: a course finishes (turns black) only after everything it unlocks has finished, so the finishing order lists every course after the courses it unlocks. Reversing it gives a valid order.
steps: Build after[a] and the in-degree indeg[b] from every rule.
Pop a course and append it to the answer. For each course it unlocks, lower the in-degree, and queue it when it reaches 0.
If the answer has n courses, return it. Otherwise return [].
pitfalls: Returning the partial order when there is a loop. The answer must be all courses or nothing, as in example 2.
Leaving out courses that appear in no rule. They have in-degree 0 and belong in the order, as course 2 does in example 3.
In the DFS version, returning the finishing order without reversing it. That lists every course after the ones it unlocks, which is backwards.

solutions.title: DFS finishing order, reversed (iterative)
solutions.idea: Three-colour DFS. When a course turns black, everything it unlocks is already black, so appending at that moment and reversing at the end gives a valid order. A grey neighbour means a loop.

solutions.title: Kahn's algorithm
solutions.idea: Repeatedly take a course with no open rules. The order they come out of the queue is the answer; fewer than n means a loop.

followups: Return the smallest order in dictionary order. What replaces the queue?
If there is a loop, return the courses that form it. How does the DFS version find them?
